title: Different Roads, Same Destination
about: What happens when pieces take different routes or get lost.

cards.title: The internet makes no promises
cards.body: [[Routers|router]] keep updating their [[routing tables|routing-table]]: if a cable breaks or a road gets busy, they find another way round. So packets from one message can arrive in a **different order**, and some never arrive. Yet your photos turn up perfectly. How?

cards.prompt: The cable from **Router A** to the [[server]] is cut (it's gone from the map). Get the [[packet]] there another way.
cards.explanation: Either detour works: via **Router B**, or via Router A and **Router C**. But packets on different roads may arrive in a different order.
cards.hint: Only follow the links you can see; there's more than one way round.
cards.nudge: Every step must follow a line on the map: [[Router]] A's direct link to the server is gone.

cards.prompt: These [[packets|packet]] took different roads and arrived jumbled. Put them back in order by **sequence number**.
cards.explanation: By sequence number they read *YOUR PIZZA IS ARRIVING*. The order they arrive in doesn't matter: the numbers say where each piece belongs.
cards.hint: The arrival order is no help: what did the sender put on every packet?
cards.nudge: Sort by the number after the #, smallest first: the arrival order doesn't matter.

cards.prompt: With **TCP** rules, the receiver reports which numbered packets arrived, and gaps are resent. Of packets 1 to 7, **1, 2, 4, 6 and 7** arrived: how many will TCP resend?
cards.explanation: Packets **3 and 5** are missing, so **2** are resent and slotted in. IP gets packets across the internet; TCP makes sure they all arrive, in order.
cards.hint: Write out 1 to 7, cross off each one that arrived, and count what's left.
cards.nudge: There may be more than one gap: check every number from 1 to 7.

cards.prompt: Match each problem to how the internet deals with it.

pairs.left: A cable on the route breaks

cards.explanation: Sequence numbers **sort** jumbled packets, [[TCP]] **resends** a missing one, and routers [[update]] their tables to **go another way** round a break.
cards.hint: Which fix uses sequence numbers, which one resends, and which is a job for routers?
cards.nudge: Only one fix happens out on the road, between routers: start with that one.

cards.prompt: A lost packet makes a video call glitch, but the call doesn't wait for a resend. Why?

options.text: Waiting would lag it; fresh data beats late
Calls are one stream, not packets
options.nudge: Everything online travels in packets, video calls included.
Any packet can go missing: the question says one did.

options.text: Video packets are too big to resend
options.nudge: Size isn't the reason: what happens to a live call while it waits?

cards.explanation: In a live call, late data is useless because that moment has passed, so apps skip lost packets, often using simpler rules called **UDP**. A download needs every [[byte]] perfect, so [[TCP]] waits and resends.
cards.hint: What use is a picture from half a second ago that turns up late?

cards.prompt: Run `traceroute example.com` and compare its [[hop|hop]]s with yesterday's [[traceroute]], above.

commands.description: List each router between you and example.com, right now

success.question: Which router's address is new today?

cards.explanation: Hop 3 changed from `203.0.113.65` to `203.0.113.129`: maybe the old [[router]] was busy or being repaired. The detour is a bit slower (22 ms to the end instead of 19), but your [[packets|packet]] still arrive.
cards.hint: Compare the address on each numbered line with yesterday's, one line at a time.
cards.nudge: The times always change a little, so compare only the addresses, and give today's new one.

cards.title: Recap: Packets and Routing
cards.body:
- Routes can change, so packets may arrive jumbled or go missing.
- **Sequence numbers** put the pieces back in order.
- **TCP** gets any missing packet sent again.
